questions.explanation: Carbon-14 dating measures radioactive decay in once-living material such as charcoal or bone.

questions.stem: A major weakness of oral tradition as a source of history is that it
options: cannot be used for pre-literate societies
is always written in foreign languages
may be distorted or exaggerated as it passes from one generation to another
questions.explanation: Oral accounts can be altered to glorify rulers or through faulty memory, so they must be cross-checked.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a written source for the history of pre-colonial Hausaland?
questions.explanation: The Kano Chronicle is an Arabic-script record of the rulers of Kano; the others are archaeological.

questions.stem: Archaeology is especially valuable for reconstructing the early history of Nigeria because
options: it relies wholly on the accounts of European travellers
it records the exact words spoken by ancient rulers
it replaces the need for oral tradition
many early societies left no written records
questions.explanation: Excavated material culture gives evidence for periods and peoples without writing.

questions.stem: The two most important commodities exchanged in the trans-Saharan trade were
options: gold from the south and salt from the north

questions.stem: Taghaza in the Sahara was famous for its
questions.explanation: Taghaza supplied rock salt carried south to the Sudan.

options: The spread of Islam and Arabic literacy
The rise of the trans-Atlantic slave trade

questions.stem: A major reason for the decline of the trans-Saharan trade was
options: the diversion of trade to the Atlantic coast by European traders
the drying up of the Sahara in the 20th century
the discovery of gold in the Sahara
questions.explanation: European coastal trade offered alternative markets and routes, alongside insecurity in the desert after the fall of Songhai.

questions.stem: Mansa Musa of Mali is famous for his pilgrimage to Mecca in
questions.explanation: His lavish pilgrimage in 1324 made Mali famous in North Africa and the Middle East.

questions.stem: Timbuktu became a great centre of Islamic learning because of
options: the Sankore mosque and its scholars
its position on the Atlantic coast
questions.explanation: The Sankore mosque and other centres attracted scholars from across the Muslim world.

questions.explanation: The Almoravid movement arose among Sanhaja Berbers and attacked ancient Ghana.

questions.explanation: Portuguese navigators explored the coast in the fifteenth century.

questions.stem: The castle of Sao Jorge da Mina (Elmina), built by the Portuguese in 1482, is located in present-day
questions.explanation: Elmina on the Gold Coast was built to protect the Portuguese gold trade.

questions.stem: The trade route which carried manufactured goods from Europe to Africa, slaves from Africa to the Americas and raw materials back to Europe is known as
questions.explanation: The three-sided pattern linked Europe, Africa and the Americas.

questions.explanation: The 1807 Act banned British participation in the slave trade.

questions.stem: Liberia, which declared its independence in 1847, was founded by
options: the British government for its soldiers
the American Colonization Society for freed African Americans

questions.topic: Christian Missionary Activities in West Africa

options: the founder of the Sokoto Caliphate
a leader of the Kiriji war
questions.explanation: Crowther, a freed slave, was consecrated bishop in 1864.

questions.topic: The Scramble for and Partition of West Africa
questions.stem: The Berlin Conference of 1884-1885 was held to
options: lay down rules for the partition of Africa among European powers
questions.explanation: European powers met in Berlin to regulate claims to African territory.

questions.topic: The Scramble for and Partition of West Africa
questions.stem: Which of the following was an economic cause of the Scramble for Africa?
options: The abolition of the Atlantic slave trade by Africans
The discovery of oil in Nigeria
The search for raw materials and markets for European industries
questions.explanation: Industrialised Europe needed raw materials, markets and investment outlets.

questions.stem: Under the French policy of assimilation in West Africa, Africans who met certain conditions could
options: be exempted from colonial rule entirely
questions.explanation: Assimilated Africans (evolues) could acquire French citizenship.

questions.stem: Which of the following was a feature of the colonial economy in West Africa?
options: Development of heavy industries in every colony
Total control of foreign trade by Africans
Production of cash crops for export
Use of a common West African currency issued by Africans
questions.explanation: Colonies produced raw materials such as cocoa, groundnuts and palm produce for European industries.

questions.topic: Problems of Independent West African States
questions.stem: Guinea became independent in 1958 after
options: fighting a long war against Britain
the collapse of the Mali Empire
voting 'No' in the French referendum on the French Community
questions.explanation: Guinea alone rejected de Gaulle's proposed Community and became independent immediately.

questions.topic: Problems of Independent West African States
questions.stem: The dispute between Nigeria and Cameroon over the Bakassi Peninsula was settled by
options: a war won by Nigeria in 1975
a judgement of the International Court of Justice in 2002
questions.explanation: The ICJ ruled in Cameroon's favour in 2002; Nigeria completed the handover in 2008 under the Greentree Agreement.

questions.topic: Problems of Independent West African States

questions.explanation: ECOWAS deployed ECOMOG in Liberia from 1990 and later in Sierra Leone.

questions.stem: The Organisation of African Unity (OAU) was replaced in 2002 by the
questions.explanation: The AU succeeded the OAU with wider goals of integration and good governance.

questions.stem: One of the achievements of the OAU was
options: supporting liberation movements against colonial and minority rule
questions.explanation: The OAU's Liberation Committee supported independence struggles and opposed apartheid.

questions.stem: The Rivers Niger and Benue meet at
questions.explanation: The confluence is at Lokoja in Kogi State.

questions.stem: The vegetation of northern Nigeria is mainly
questions.explanation: Grassland and open woodland dominate the north, favouring cattle rearing and grain crops.

options: a man digging a cistern in his compound
a British colonial officer building a road
a team from the University of Ibadan

questions.topic: Centres of Ancient Civilization in Nigeria

questions.stem: Mai Idris Alooma of Borno strengthened his army by
options: relying only on bows and arrows
questions.explanation: In the sixteenth century he obtained muskets and trainers from North Africa.

questions.stem: According to tradition, the Hausa Bakwai states were founded by the descendants of
questions.explanation: The Bayajidda legend traces the seven Hausa states to his union with the queen of Daura.

questions.stem: The Tiv of the Benue valley are an example of
questions.explanation: The Tiv governed through lineage elders without a single paramount ruler.

questions.stem: Which of the following promoted inter-group relations in pre-colonial Nigeria?
questions.explanation: Long-distance and local trade brought different peoples into contact.

options: trade networks and the Ibini Ukpabi oracle

questions.topic: Impact of Migrations, Wars and Politics
questions.stem: The Fulani jihad of the nineteenth century affected inter-group relations by
options: bringing many Hausa states under a single caliphate
questions.explanation: The jihad replaced Hausa dynasties with Fulani emirs under Sokoto.

questions.topic: Impact of Migrations, Wars and Politics
questions.stem: The Yoruba wars of the nineteenth century led to
options: mass movement of people and the founding of new towns such as Abeokuta and Ibadan
the rise of the trans-Saharan trade
the unification of all Yoruba under Benin
the end of the Atlantic slave trade
questions.explanation: Refugees from the wars founded or expanded towns like Abeokuta and Ibadan.

questions.stem: The town of Iseyin in Oyo State is famous for
questions.explanation: Iseyin is a traditional centre of aso-oke weaving.

questions.stem: The ancient dye pits of Kano were used for
questions.explanation: The Kofar Mata dye pits are among the oldest in Nigeria.

questions.stem: Bida in Nupeland was noted for
questions.explanation: Nupe craftsmen at Bida produced glass beads and brass ware.

questions.stem: The first ruler of Kanem traditionally regarded as having accepted Islam was
questions.explanation: Mai Humme (late eleventh century) is credited as the first Muslim ruler of Kanem.

questions.stem: Islam was introduced into Kano in the fourteenth century largely through
options: Wangarawa traders and scholars from Mali
questions.explanation: The Kano Chronicle records the Wangarawa arriving in the reign of Ali Yaji.

questions.topic: Early European Contact with Coastal States
questions.stem: The Portuguese first reached the kingdom of Benin in the
questions.explanation: Portuguese contact with Benin dates to the 1480s.

questions.topic: Early European Contact with Coastal States
questions.stem: Which of the following was an early effect of European contact on the coastal states of Nigeria?
options: Introduction of new crops such as maize and cassava
questions.explanation: Portuguese traders introduced American crops, firearms and other goods.

questions.topic: Nigeria and the Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade
questions.stem: Which of the following was a major slave-exporting port in Nigeria?
questions.explanation: Badagry, Lagos, Bonny and Calabar were coastal outlets for the slave trade.

questions.topic: Nigeria and the Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade
questions.stem: After the abolition of the slave trade, the main export from the Niger Delta to Europe became
questions.explanation: Palm oil for soap and lubrication became the leading 'legitimate' export.

questions.stem: The jihad that led to the establishment of the Sokoto Caliphate began in
questions.explanation: Uthman dan Fodio declared the jihad against Gobir in 1804.

questions.stem: The first Sultan of Sokoto was
questions.explanation: Bello, Uthman's son, took the title of Sultan; Abdullahi ruled the western half from Gwandu.

questions.stem: Which of the following was a reason for the jihad of Uthman dan Fodio?
options: Opposition to oppressive taxes and un-Islamic practices of the Hausa rulers
The collapse of the trans-Atlantic trade
questions.explanation: Uthman denounced injustice, heavy taxation and syncretism among Hausa rulers.

questions.stem: The scholar who defended Borno against the Sokoto jihadists in the early nineteenth century was
questions.explanation: Al-Kanemi drove back the jihadists and became the effective ruler of Borno.

questions.stem: The rule of the Shehus of Borno was disrupted in 1893 by the invasion of
questions.explanation: Rabeh, a Sudanese adventurer, conquered Borno and destroyed Kukawa.

questions.stem: Christian missionaries of the Wesleyan Methodist Mission arrived at Badagry in
questions.explanation: Thomas Birch Freeman arrived at Badagry in September 1842.

questions.stem: Mary Slessor is remembered for her work among the people of
questions.explanation: She worked to end the killing of twins and to promote welfare.

questions.stem: The Church of Scotland Mission which began work in Calabar in 1846 was led by
questions.explanation: Rev. Hope Waddell led the mission; the Hope Waddell Training Institute is named after him.

questions.stem: The collapse of the Old Oyo Empire occurred in the
questions.explanation: Old Oyo was abandoned around 1835-1836 after attacks linked to Ilorin.

questions.stem: The revolt of Afonja, the Are-Ona-Kakanfo, contributed to the fall of Oyo by
options: leading to the loss of Ilorin to the Fulani jihadists
ending the slave trade in Yorubaland
questions.explanation: Afonja's rebellion at Ilorin opened the way for the Fulani to take control there.

questions.stem: At the Battle of Osogbo in 1840, Ibadan forces
options: defeated the Ilorin army and halted the Fulani advance into Yorubaland
questions.explanation: The victory checked Ilorin's southward expansion.

questions.stem: The Oba of Benin at the time of the British conquest of 1897 was
questions.explanation: Oba Ovonramwen was deposed and exiled to Calabar after the British expedition.

questions.stem: A long-term effect of the 1897 British expedition on Benin was
options: the removal of thousands of Benin bronzes and ivories to Europe
the creation of the Sokoto Caliphate
the abolition of the Oba's title for ever
the transfer of Benin to French control
questions.explanation: Many artworks were taken as war booty; some have begun to be returned in recent years.

questions.topic: The First Phase of the British Conquest of Nigeria, 1851-1900

questions.explanation: King Dosunmu signed the treaty of cession in August 1861.

questions.topic: The First Phase of the British Conquest of Nigeria, 1851-1900
questions.stem: The British bombardment of Lagos in 1851 resulted in
options: the removal of Kosoko and the restoration of Akitoye
the annexation of Lagos as a colony
the end of the Sokoto jihad
questions.explanation: Britain intervened, citing the slave trade, and reinstated Akitoye.

questions.topic: The First Phase of the British Conquest of Nigeria, 1851-1900

questions.stem: The Sokoto Caliphate was conquered by British forces under Lugard in

questions.stem: Coal mining began in Nigeria at
questions.explanation: Coal was discovered near Enugu in 1909 and mining began in 1915.

questions.stem: Which of the following was a feature of the colonial economy in Nigeria between 1914 and 1960?
options: Use of the Naira as currency
Emphasis on the export of cash crops like cocoa, groundnuts and palm produce
questions.explanation: The economy was oriented towards exporting primary produce.

questions.stem: Regional self-government was granted to the Western and Eastern Regions in
questions.explanation: The West and East became self-governing in 1957; the North in 1959.

questions.stem: The Northern Region attained self-government in
questions.explanation: The North was the last region to gain self-government.

questions.stem: Nigeria became a republic in
questions.explanation: The Republican Constitution came into force on 1 October 1963.

questions.stem: The Mid-Western Region was created in
questions.explanation: It was carved out of the Western Region after a referendum in 1963.

questions.stem: The Naira and Kobo replaced the Nigerian pound as currency in
questions.explanation: Decimal currency was introduced on 1 January 1973.

questions.stem: Nigeria became a member of the United Nations in
questions.explanation: Nigeria was admitted on 7 October 1960, shortly after independence.

questions.stem: Nigeria joined the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) in
questions.explanation: Nigeria became OPEC's eleventh member in 1971.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a global issue?
options: The election of a local council chairman
questions.explanation: Global issues affect many countries and need international cooperation.

questions.stem: The Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) adopted by the UN in 2015 are meant to be achieved by
questions.explanation: The 2030 Agenda contains 17 SDGs that replaced the Millennium Development Goals.

questions.stem: The shrinking of Lake Chad has been caused mainly by
options: reduced rainfall and increased water use for irrigation
questions.explanation: Drought and human water use have reduced the lake, harming livelihoods in the region.

questions.topic: Centres of Ancient Civilization in Nigeria
questions.stem:
(a) Describe five features of the Nok culture. [10 marks]
(b) Explain how archaeology has contributed to the knowledge of ancient civilisations in Nigeria. [5 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: Located in the central Nigerian area (southern Kaduna/Plateau/Nasarawa), first identified at Nok village
2 marks: Famous for terracotta (baked clay) sculptures of human heads and figures
2 marks: Evidence of early iron smelting and iron tools, e.g. at Taruga
2 marks: Dated to the first millennium BC and early centuries AD
2 marks: Stylised features such as pierced eyes and elaborate hairstyles, showing skilled artistry and settled farming communities
3 marks: Excavations at Nok, Igbo-Ukwu, Ife and Benin uncovered artefacts that reveal technology, art, trade and social organisation of peoples without written records
2 marks: Dating methods such as radiocarbon dating give the age of sites and artefacts
questions.explanation: Nok in central Nigeria produced distinctive terracotta sculptures and early iron-working from the first millennium BC. Archaeology, through excavation and dating, has revealed the art, technology and trade of ancient Nigerian societies that left no written records.

questions.stem:
(a) Describe the political organisation of the Kanem-Borno empire under the Saifawa dynasty. [9 marks]
(b) Explain three achievements of Mai Idris Alooma. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: The Mai was the head of the empire, regarded as semi-divine and assisted by a council of state
2 marks: The Magira (queen mother) and other royal women held important offices
2 marks: Provinces were administered by title-holders/fief holders who collected tribute
2 marks: Islamic law influenced administration and justice, with Alkalis serving as judges
1 mark: A strong army of cavalry protected the state
2 marks: Acquired firearms and Turkish musketeers to modernise the army
2 marks: Expanded and consolidated the empire through military campaigns
2 marks: Promoted Islam and Islamic law, built mosques and performed the pilgrimage, or improved diplomacy with North Africa
questions.explanation: Saifawa Borno was ruled by a semi-divine Mai with a council, influential royal women, provincial fief-holders, Islamic judges and a strong cavalry. Idris Alooma modernised the army with firearms, expanded the empire and strengthened Islam and diplomacy.

questions.stem:
(a) Name three items exported from West Africa and three items imported from North Africa in the trans-Saharan trade. [6 marks]
(b) Explain three effects of the trans-Saharan trade on West Africa. [9 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark: Export: gold
1 mark: Export: slaves
1 mark: Export: kola nuts, ivory or leather goods
1 mark: Import: salt
1 mark: Import: horses
1 mark: Import: textiles, books, swords or copper
3 marks: Spread of Islam and Arabic literacy along the trade routes
3 marks: Rise of wealthy states and cities such as Ghana, Mali, Songhai, Kano and Borno
3 marks: Introduction of new goods and ideas, or the growth of a class of wealthy traders
questions.explanation: West Africa exported gold, slaves, kola and ivory and imported salt, horses, cloth and books. The trade spread Islam and literacy, enriched states and cities and introduced new goods and ideas.

questions.stem:
(a) Explain five causes of the Sokoto jihad of 1804. [10 marks]
(b) State five effects of the jihad on Hausaland. [5 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: Uthman dan Fodio's preaching against the mixing of Islam with traditional practices
2 marks: Heavy and un-Islamic taxes such as the cattle tax (jangali) and market tolls
2 marks: Injustice, corruption and oppression by Hausa rulers
2 marks: Conflict with the rulers of Gobir, who tried to restrict Uthman's community
2 marks: Influence of earlier Islamic reform movements, or grievances of Fulani herdsmen
1 mark: Establishment of the Sokoto Caliphate under one central authority
1 mark: Replacement of Hausa rulers by Fulani emirs
1 mark: Spread and purification of Islam and Islamic law
1 mark: Growth of Islamic learning and literacy
1 mark: Loss of lives and property, or migration of peoples, or creation of new emirates
questions.explanation: The jihad arose from religious syncretism, oppressive taxes, injustice and conflict with Gobir. It created the Sokoto Caliphate, installed Fulani emirs, spread Islam and learning, but caused loss of lives and dislocation.

questions.stem:
(a) Explain five reasons for the collapse of the Old Oyo Empire. [10 marks]
(b) State five consequences of the collapse of Old Oyo on Yorubaland. [5 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: Constitutional conflict between the Alaafin and the Oyomesi, e.g. the Bashorun Gaa episode
2 marks: Revolt of Afonja, the Are-Ona-Kakanfo, at Ilorin
2 marks: Fulani jihadists' takeover of Ilorin and attacks on Oyo
2 marks: Revolt of vassal states such as Egba and Dahomey
2 marks: Decline in trade revenue, especially after the abolition of the slave trade, or the size of the empire
1 mark: Outbreak of the Yoruba civil wars
1 mark: Rise of new powers such as Ibadan, Ijaye and Abeokuta
1 mark: Mass migration and founding of new towns, including New Oyo
1 mark: Increase in slave raiding and insecurity
1 mark: Opened the way for British intervention
questions.explanation: Oyo fell through internal power struggles, Afonja's revolt, the Fulani at Ilorin, vassal revolts and loss of trade. Its collapse brought civil wars, new powers like Ibadan and Abeokuta, migrations, insecurity and British intervention.

questions.stem:
(a) Name three Christian missionary bodies that worked in Nigeria in the nineteenth century. [3 marks]
(b) Explain four contributions of Christian missionaries to the development of Nigeria. [8 marks]
(c) State two problems missionaries faced in Nigeria. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark: Wesleyan Methodist Mission
1 mark: Church Missionary Society (CMS)
1 mark: Church of Scotland Mission, Southern Baptist Mission or Roman Catholic Society of African Missions
2 marks: Introduction of Western education and schools such as CMS Grammar School, Lagos
2 marks: Provision of health care through hospitals and dispensaries
2 marks: Reduction of practices such as the killing of twins
2 marks: Development of written forms of local languages and printing, e.g. Iwe Irohin
2 marks: Tropical diseases such as malaria that killed many missionaries
2 marks: Opposition from traditional rulers and religious leaders, or poor transport and communication
questions.explanation: Methodists, the CMS, the Church of Scotland, Baptists and Catholics spread Christianity, schools, hospitals, literacy and social reform, but faced disease, local opposition and poor communication.

questions.topic: The First Phase of the British Conquest of Nigeria, 1851-1900
questions.stem:
(a) Give an account of the relationship between Jaja of Opobo and the British up to 1887. [10 marks]
(b) Explain two reasons why the British were able to defeat Nigerian resistance in the nineteenth century. [5 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: Jaja rose from slave origins to head the Anna Pepple House in Bonny
2 marks: Following a dispute in Bonny he founded Opobo in 1869 and controlled the palm oil trade of the hinterland
2 marks: Britain recognised Opobo by a treaty in 1873
2 marks: Jaja insisted on his right to tax and control trade, and resisted British traders' attempts to deal directly with the hinterland producers
2 marks: Consul Harry Johnston lured him aboard a ship in 1887, tried him and deported him to the West Indies
3 marks: Superior British weapons such as the Maxim gun
2 marks: Disunity among Nigerian states, or British use of African troops and treaties
questions.explanation: Jaja founded Opobo in 1869, dominated the palm-oil trade and was recognised by treaty in 1873, but his defence of his middleman position clashed with British free-trade aims and he was deported in 1887. British victories owed much to superior weapons and Nigerian disunity.

questions.stem:
(a) Explain four reasons for the amalgamation of Northern and Southern Nigeria in 1914. [8 marks]
(b) Explain three consequences of the amalgamation. [6 marks]
(c) Name the Governor-General who carried out the amalgamation. [1 mark]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: Economic: to use the surplus revenue of the South to offset the deficit of the North
2 marks: Administrative convenience and reduction of costs
2 marks: Need for a unified railway and transport system
2 marks: Need for uniform policies, or to link the North to the sea for trade
2 marks: Creation of Nigeria as one political unit
2 marks: Unequal development, as North and South continued to be administered differently
2 marks: Extension of indirect rule to the South, or the beginning of ethnic and regional rivalry
1 mark: Frederick Lugard
questions.explanation: Amalgamation in 1914 aimed to balance revenue, cut costs, unify transport and harmonise policy. It created Nigeria but left uneven development and extended indirect rule southwards. Lugard carried it out.

questions.stem:
(a) Explain five factors that contributed to the growth of nationalism in Nigeria after 1945. [10 marks]
(b) Mention five constitutional steps that led to Nigeria's independence in 1960. [5 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: Return of ex-servicemen from the Second World War with new ideas
2 marks: Activities of educated elites and the nationalist press
2 marks: Formation of political parties such as the NCNC, AG and NPC
2 marks: Economic hardship and discrimination under colonial rule
2 marks: Influence of the Atlantic Charter, Indian independence (1947) and the Pan-African movement
1 mark: Clifford Constitution 1922 (elective principle)
1 mark: Richards Constitution 1946 (regionalism)
1 mark: Macpherson Constitution 1951 (wide consultation)
1 mark: Lyttleton Constitution 1954 (federalism)
1 mark: Regional self-government 1957/1959 and the 1957-1958 constitutional conferences
questions.explanation: Post-war nationalism grew through ex-servicemen, the elite and the press, parties, economic grievances and international influences. Independence came through the 1922, 1946, 1951 and 1954 constitutions, regional self-government and the London conferences.

questions.stem:
(a) Explain five causes of the Nigerian civil war of 1967-1970. [10 marks]
(b) State five effects of the civil war on Nigeria. [5 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: The January 1966 coup and its perceived ethnic character
2 marks: The July 1966 counter-coup and killings of easterners in the North
2 marks: Failure to implement the Aburi Accord of January 1967
2 marks: Creation of twelve states in May 1967, which the Eastern Region rejected
2 marks: Declaration of the Republic of Biafra by the Eastern Region on 30 May 1967, or disputes over oil revenue
1 mark: Loss of lives and property
1 mark: Displacement of people and refugee problems
1 mark: Strengthening of the central government
1 mark: Introduction of reconciliation, rehabilitation and reconstruction policies and the NYSC (1973)
1 mark: Proliferation of arms, or economic disruption
questions.explanation: The war followed the 1966 coups and killings, the failure of Aburi, the twelve-state creation and the secession of the East. It caused heavy loss of life and displacement, strengthened the centre and led to reconciliation programmes such as the NYSC.
